title: One gene, several proteins by alternative splicing

stimulus.title: Two mRNAs from one gene
stimulus.html: A human gene has five exons. Muscle cells and nerve cells both transcribe the gene, but the mature mRNAs differ, as shown. The two mRNAs code for related but different proteins.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe what happens to the introns of this gene's pre-mRNA, and where in the cell it happens.

rubric.point: Describes that the introns are cut out of the pre-mRNA (by spliceosomes) and the exons are joined, in the nucleus, before the mRNA is exported.
accept: spliceosomes remove the introns and join exons in the nucleus
introns are spliced out of the RNA in the nucleus
introns cut out of pre-mRNA before it leaves the nucleus

parts.sample: In the nucleus, spliceosomes cut the four introns out of the pre-mRNA and join the exons together. The introns are broken down, and the mature mRNA, with its cap and tail, leaves through the nuclear pores.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain how the same gene produces different proteins in muscle cells and nerve cells.

rubric.point: Explains alternative splicing: the same pre-mRNA is spliced differently in the two cell types, so muscle mRNA includes exon 3 and nerve mRNA includes exon 4; the different exon sequences give proteins with different amino acid sequences.
accept: alternative splicing includes exon 3 in muscle and exon 4 in nerve, so the proteins differ
different exons are joined in each cell type, changing the protein's sequence
the pre-mRNA is the same but is spliced in two ways

parts.sample: By alternative splicing. Both cell types make the same pre-mRNA, but muscle cells join exons 1, 2, 3 and 5 while nerve cells join exons 1, 2, 4 and 5. Exons 3 and 4 code for different stretches of amino acids, so the two mRNAs give proteins that share most of their sequence but differ in one part.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: A change in the DNA destroys the splicing signal at the start of exon 4, so exon 4 can no longer be included in any mRNA. Predict the effect on the protein made in each cell type.

rubric.point: Predicts that muscle cells are unaffected (their mRNA, exons 1-2-3-5, never included exon 4), while nerve cells cannot make their normal protein (their mRNA would lack exon 4, for example 1-2-5, giving a shorter, altered protein, or a defective mRNA).
accept: muscle protein normal; nerve protein missing the exon 4 part
only nerve cells are affected because muscle mRNA does not use exon 4
nerve cells would make a 1-2-5 mRNA and an abnormal protein, muscle cells unchanged

parts.sample: Muscle cells would make their normal protein, because their mRNA (exons 1, 2, 3, 5) never includes exon 4. Nerve cells could not include exon 4, so they would make an mRNA with exons 1, 2 and 5 (or a faulty mRNA), and their protein would lack the part coded by exon 4 and probably not work normally.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Justify the claim that the difference between the muscle and nerve proteins does not require any difference in the cells' DNA.

rubric.point: Justifies with the model/data: both cell types carry and transcribe the same gene (same exons and introns); the difference arises after transcription, in which exons are kept during splicing, so the DNA sequence is identical.
accept: both cells have the same five-exon gene; only the splicing differs
the difference is made in RNA processing, after transcription, not in the DNA
the same pre-mRNA is made in both cells, so the DNA is the same

parts.sample: Both cell types carry the same gene with the same five exons and four introns and transcribe it into the same pre-mRNA. The difference appears afterward, when splicing keeps exon 3 in muscle cells and exon 4 in nerve cells. So the proteins differ because of RNA processing, not because of any difference in the DNA.
